Main should not need to know details of the devices, only collect their interfaces.' choice: order module-level constants by who changes the value, tunable first, developer-only bindings last
note: Raised against owned/acme.py in benchmark/round7/programs/level_test/, where DEVICES sat below the function definitions next to VENDOR. Verbatim: 'in acme/tesla, DEVICES are user input constants, which means it needs to go at the top of the file with other constants. VENDOR is a code interface thing and would only normally be changed by the developer, so it going at the bottom of the file is fine.' This sharpens two rules the style already has. R3a-12 asks whether someone could change a value knowing only what the program DOES, and uses that to decide module level against function local; the same question also decides ORDER within the module-level block. SKILL.md already separates tunable constants from design-baked globals with a blank line, and the real criterion behind that separation is who does the changing, not global against constant. Note the collision and its resolution: DEVICES is the most operator-facing constant in the file, so it wants to be first, but its value references ACME_FORMAT and RETRY_CAP_S, so module execution order forces it last inside the block. It joins the constant block rather than leading it. That is R4-03's precedent exactly -- ordering is forced by execution and you do not contort around it. Three-part shape for a library module that follows: tunable constants, then the functions, then the interface binding that names them.

options: two files, split only where a second program needs the code

condition: for this program; the general rule is to cut on whichever axis the expected changes land in more cleanly

A handles this gracefully with minimal LOC changes.' a named module for the shared one, the other two stay local

A helper that crosses a boundary must be findable by someone who did not write it, which forces it to name a concept; one that never leaves does not. NOTE THE UNTESTED PREDICTION: the two tests are claimed identical and no case where they disagree has been built. Build one before this ships as a rule.

options: the package glossary holds every type, crossing or not
the glossary holds what crosses, a single-module type stays home

If it is likely to be read by other scripts, moving it pre-emptively to common is a good idea.' Moving a type later changes every import of it and is a mechanical, reviewable edit that a type checker verifies; a wrongly-general dispatch mechanism is load-bearing and its removal is not mechanical. A checker can enforce the pair exactly -- a cross-module import of an underscore-prefixed name is a mechanical finding with no judgement in it -- which makes this one of the few architecture answers in round 7 that is lintable.

options: service.py holds main and __main__.py re-exports it

Generally it should hold the primary entrypoint for the module, but if it gets too long it can be split out to another file.' The dunder never reaches a user, who types the package name. options: exempt until the second public function

If the file has only a single function, the file-wide docstring can be skipped.' options: one public function, underscore names do not count
one public function and also short

The second def, of any kind, makes the docstring mandatory. The line-count variant was rejected, consistent with R7-B01-B03-criterion having just removed size as a criterion. Checkable exactly by counting FunctionDef and AsyncFunctionDef at module level. Still unsettled and NOT decided here: whether a runnable module is exempt, since NAR009's other clause demands a usage example from anything with a __main__ block. Settle that before checks.py changes.

Scope for the underscore convention chosen in R7-B08. It marks any module-level name -- functions, constants, classes, type aliases -- so _FRAME_FORMAT and _FrameHeader are as legitimate as _unpackFields. A module FILENAME does not take the underscore; the third option offering _helpers.py was not chosen. The churn objection was put and rejected on its own terms, verbatim: 'I reject the framing of costs churn: a name that becomes public later gets renamed at every call site. If it is getting called in a bunch of places, it is public, not private.' That reply is the more portable finding. The underscore is a statement of present fact, not a forecast, so a name whose fact changes SHOULD be renamed and the rename is the correct signal rather than a cost. Contrast R7-B07-preemption, where a TYPE may be centralised on a forecast -- the asymmetry is that centralising a type is reversible mechanically and a privacy claim is not a claim about the future at all.

Answers what replaces the single-file reading order once R7-B01 splits a program into six modules. The thesis stays with main(): __main__.py opens with a docstring naming what the program is for and listing the modules in reading order, and every other module keeps its own one-line docstring. The stated model, verbatim: 'My understanding is __init__ is for startup stuff that needs to run as a consequence of module import. __main__.py is new to me, I hadn't heard about it, but it more or less seems to replace what I previously had as main.py.' Known and accepted cost: a reader arriving at store.py from a stack trace or a grep sees one line about that file and nothing telling them five siblings exist or where to start. Most readers do not arrive at the entry point. The alternative of a back-pointer per module was offered and not chosen. See R7-B01-init for the checker consequence.

choice: an empty __init__.py needs no docstring; NAR009 needs a second exemption
note: Found by building rather than by asking, which is the GAPS.md method. benchmark/round7/programs/six_modules/ is the first program in this repository with an __init__.py, and checks.py immediately reported collector/__init__.py:1: NAR009 module has no docstring. An empty __init__.py is the ordinary correct thing for an application package once R7-B01-map puts the reading order in __main__.py. Note this is NOT covered by the exemption in R7-B10-scope, which is worded as exactly one def; an empty __init__.py has none. So NAR009 now carries two pending change requests: exempt a module with exactly one def, and exempt an __init__.py. Neither is implemented in this round -- the acceptance gate requires a cost measurement first. Contrast R7-B05, where a LIBRARY package's __init__.py is a re-export facade and does carry a docstring; the two are not in conflict, because that one has content.

options: it must appear in a signature first
name it but leave it local
choice: it must appear in a signature first
note: Bounds R7-B07, which said types centralise pre-emptively and which taken literally would send every shape in a program to the glossary. It does not reach the three values struct.unpack produces inside parseFrame. Verbatim: 'The struct is never observed anywhere else, only inside parseFrame. As long as the output has guarantees on typing, it is kosher.' So the test is mechanical and checkable: a shape that appears in a parameter or return annotation is a type the program has and centralises; a shape built and consumed inside one function is a step, not a type. This keeps the glossary an inventory of what modules pass between them rather than of every intermediate value, and it reconciles R7-B07 with R7-A05-property -- a purely internal shape is a property of the function that builds it.

VERIFIED BLOCKED. ruff format rewrites the preferred form to its own and exposes no setting for it, being Black-compatible and Black having deliberately no continuation-indent knob. The DRY framing is an argument R2-01 does not carry -- a Protocol over the only implementation restates every method signature, so it is a cost paid now rather than a benefit merely deferred. Offered as an addition to the rule and REJECTED as a restatement: 'The Protocol fails in this case because it is only consumed by one thing. Adding another statement saying it violates DRY would be strictly true, but also be a unnecessary duplication of the same problem description.' Verbatim: 'A is preferred because a database bring up and bring down has an associated lifetime and entry/exit method, so scoping it inside a class makes sense.' The class is justified by lifetime ownership, not by polymorphism, which is why it survives alongside R7-C01 refusing the Protocol. Consistent with R7-A03: the entry point still opens the resource and passes the object down.

choice: a class is earned by owning a lifetime; a Protocol is earned by a second real implementation
note: SUPERSEDED by R7-C01-C02-revised. The lifetime-ownership criterion below was REJECTED: 'I do not think R7-C01's conclusion of objects can only exist if they own a lifetime is right.' The half about Protocols stands. Original record follows. Reconciles R7-C01, R7-C02 and R7-C08, which chose no-Protocol, yes-object and real-dependencies in the same block. Two separate tests that look similar and are not. A class exists because something has a bring-up and a bring-down, or state that must stay consistent, and something must own that. A Protocol exists only when a second real implementation exists, and a test double is not one (R2-02). So the single-implementer check proposed for arch_checks.py would be the RIGHT check for Protocols and the WRONG one for classes, and any such rule must say which it counts. The alternative reading, that the object is justified by cohesion rather than lifetime, was offered and not chosen.

options: each stage decides and calls the next
one coordinator calls each stage and holds the intermediates
choice: one coordinator calls each stage and holds the intermediates
note: Verbatim: 'verifyAndStore and storeAndReport are not going to be reused anywhere else, so splitting it like this adds a bunch of argument passing and function signature for no reason.' Direct application of R2-09 (extract on foreseen reuse, not on nameability) and of R7-M02 (a threaded parameter is the dearest cost). CONFOUND, self-reported and real: 'verifyAndStore and storeAndReport are not great function names or logical cut points, which is biasing me against A.' Both are and-names, which signal a function doing two things, so option A was weaker than the dimension it was meant to test. The stated exception survives the confound and is the portable half: 'I can see splitting a clearly logically disconnected complicated piece in a function to keep an implementation clear.' So chained delegation is refused for a pipeline whose stages are arbitrary cuts, not for a genuinely separable piece.

note: Verbatim: 'Sending arguments to functions that do not use them is generally a waste of mental RAM (unless they are wrapped in a larger config).' Restates R7-M02 from a third direction and confirms it at module scale. Note the parenthetical, which is the seed of the R7-C05 question: bundling several such values into one named config is an accepted escape from the cost, and it is what makes a context object defensible where a loose parameter is not.

options: a pure decision, then one executor
choice: a pure decision, then one executor
note: Provocation LANDED, reversing the round-3 P1 result at a size where the plan record pays. Four routing rules and three effects. Verbatim: 'I like B a lot more, it separates out the logically coherent pieces.' Round 3 ranked the pure-core variant THIRD, and the recorded reason there was about global state rather than about purity, so this is the first clean test of the axis. Read with R7-C07, which refuses the same split at a smaller size: the pair yields a threshold rather than a flat rule, which was the stated aim of asking twice.

Verbatim: 'At this size, B is fine, but if renderRound were doing a bunch of unwieldy logic rather than a simple f-string, it may make sense to do A.' So the pure-core split is not a flat rule: it is earned by the amount of decision-making in the pure part. One f-string is not a core. Four routing rules is. R2-09's one-line-helper-called-once-is-residue is the same judgement at function scale, and this extends it to the pure-core pattern.

CONTROL PASSED, first time, no re-ask. Reproduces R2-02 in a question that also changes the production signature from a connection to a store object. Verbatim: 'A is preferred as it exercises real functionality. A test can drift from the underlying implementation, you never want to be testing your test harness rather than the real code functionality.' Note the answer went to A while R7-C02 chose the store OBJECT, so the vote is against the double specifically and not against the seam -- the two are consistent, and the reconciliation is R7-C01-C02.

choice: if a general name for the group is hard to pick, it is not a real grouping
note: R7-C05 as asked was rejected as an instrument: 'I do not really understand how Collection is a clear descriptor of something that holds both a SQL connection, a device mapping, and a path. Since this dataclass sucks, I am biased towards A, but I think that just indicates that this test is a poor discriminator.' Correct, and the failure is the finding. Verbatim on the reframe: 'if picking a general name is really hard, it probably isn't a proper grouping.' This is the guard rail R2b-E3 lacks. That rule says 5+ parameters means a missing state dataclass; it does not say what to do when the five do not name anything, which is the common case. Whether the remedy is then a better-named bundle or a missing OWNER is unsettled -- see the open note on R7-C05.

options: not where the name only echoes
condition: the size at which it starts to matter is unmeasured; the reasoning was given for a 50-line function
note: Raised unprompted while reading benchmark/round7/programs/six_modules/. The preference is `plan = RecordPlan(...)` then `return plan` over returning the constructor call. RET504 forbids exactly this and is ALREADY DISABLED (R6-06), on reasoning the answerer re-derived independently -- a named intermediate tells the reader what is being returned. So unlike R7-indent this preference is implementable; the config permitted it and no rule stated it. Asked as always / only-where-informative / only-the-last-return, and measured first against the running program: 13 of 14 returns would gain a line under always, including three near-identical `outcome = ...` / `return outcome` pairs inside one function, which manufactures the rote diffing R2b-P0 exists to prevent, and `read = sum(...)` inside a property already named read. The answer narrows to the FINAL return only, and the stated reason is orientation rather than naming: 'if a function is 50 lines long, figuring out what the return type should be requires scrolling all the way back up to the function signature. If there is simply a descriptive name at the end then it is clear what it is supposed to be returning.' Early returns and guard exits are therefore exempt, which removes the three-identical-pairs cost entirely. Mechanically checkable -- a checker can tell the final statement of a body from an early exit. OPEN: the reasoning is about a long function and no threshold was set, so whether a three-line function's final return needs a name is unsettled. NAR004 has the precedent, requiring a docstring once a body runs past 20 lines.

options: values that could differ between instances
the group has a domain noun
choice: values that could differ between instances
note: Replaces the lifetime-ownership criterion of R7-C01-C02, which was rejected, and the shared-state criterion offered next, which was rejected as too loose: 'I like shared state several operations need but I do not think it is anywhere near specific enough. Every file would be a class under this rule.' Correct -- almost every module has functions sharing a topic and some values. The criterion that survives: a CLASS when the values come from outside and the program could hold two of them at once, a MODULE when the values are constants of the program. ReadingStore qualifies, because two connections can coexist. RetentionPolicy qualifies, because per-site policies can coexist. protocol.py does not, because FRAME_FORMAT and MAGIC are the same everywhere. checksum.py does not. The Protocol half of R7-C01-C02 is untouched and still stands: a Protocol is earned by a second real implementation and a test double is not one (R2-02). Note this also DISSOLVES an apparent conflict. options: every bundle is a missing class

note: The forced choice as put was malformed and was called out: 'C and B here are not mutually exclusive options since they do not work on the same code.' Correct -- the two rewrites applied to two different signatures, so they could never compete. The synthesis, once the class criterion of R7-C01-C02-revised is in hand: a long parameter list is a missing OWNER, not a missing record. Find what owns the values. That owner is a class when the program could hold two of it, and a module otherwise. pollOne(connection, devices, status_path, device) becomes pollOne(store, device) because a store owns all three and two stores can coexist. pruneOldReadings(connection, retention_days, prune_batch, now) becomes a method on RetentionPolicy for the same reason. This rewrites R2b-E3, which says 5+ parameters means a missing state dataclass: it usually means a missing owner, and the dataclass is only the answer when nothing has behaviour over the values. The naming guard rail from R7-C05-naming still applies -- if a general name for the group is hard to pick, it is not a real grouping.

the name is wrong, not the scope

I prefer verbose function names generally speaking.' The defect is not that the name is short or unqualified. cutoffFor says what the function takes; it should say what it returns, which is the instant before which readings are deleted, so deleteBefore or oldestReadingToKeep. Verbosity was the symptom the answerer reported and naming the RESULT is the cure, so lengthening a label is the wrong fix. This is new. Q11 covers abbreviations and Q12 covers predicates; nothing in the style says a name should describe the output. It also removes the pressure R7-B06 would otherwise create, where a module-qualified call invites shorter and vaguer function names.

sqlite3 appears in exactly one module

note: Provocation REFUTED. The argument put was that a store module owning every query is the ceremony the no-ORM rule exists to reject, so the raw handle should cross freely. Verbatim: 'B is strongly preferred, downstream logic handlers should not have to explicitly pass around a sqlite3 lifetime object.' Q17's objection is to pervasive runtime validation, not to containment, so the two never actually conflicted. Consistent with R7-C02, which made the store an object, and with R7-C05-resolved, which reads a long parameter list as a missing owner -- three questions in two blocks converging on the same answer from different directions.

Verbatim: 'A is preferred because it is simpler and comes with more batteries installed (which means easier to extend in the future).' So the style is not stdlib-absolutist, and the test is simplicity at the call site plus headroom, not import count. Extends R2-06, which took python-decouple over os.environ. The question stated its own confound: B raises its own error type where A lets httpx raise, and B needs asyncio.to_thread because urllib blocks and R2-04 makes the program async. Both costs are inherent to choosing the standard library here, and the answer was given with them attached.

options: call httpx where it is needed
note: Verbatim: 'I like B because it keeps the connection related logic in one place, and the downstream functions only have to think about the actual function logic rather than the connection bookkeeping.' Read with R7-D02 the policy is two steps and they do not conflict: TAKE the dependency when it is simpler, then CONTAIN it so only one module names it. See R7-D01-D03-containment for the general rule and its limit.

note: Generalises R7-D01 and R7-D03. A live HANDLE -- a connection, an HTTP client, a socket -- appears in signatures only inside the module that owns it, and everything downstream sees a domain type. A third-party VALUE type is not contained: datetime, Decimal, a numpy array in a numeric program may cross freely, because wrapping them buys nothing and costs a conversion at every boundary. The criterion is lifetime, not provenance. Note lifetime returns here after being REJECTED as the criterion for whether a class should exist (R7-C01-C02-revised); the two are different questions and there is no contradiction, but the coincidence is worth recording so the rules are not merged later. That list is a fact about libraries rather than a claim about this program's design, which is why it does not fall to R7-A05-levels' rejection of declared layer tables.

no exception, it becomes a separate program

The performance half does not survive checking. Free-threading and the JIT are properties of the BUILD, not of the language level: verified on the machine here, which runs 3.14.4 with Py_GIL_DISABLED False, because the GIL-free interpreter is a separate binary (python3.14t). On the versions themselves: in 3.13 both features are experimental, free-threading needs a separate build and cost roughly 40% single-threaded early on, and the JIT is opt-in at build time with small and sometimes negative gains; free-threading is only officially supported at 3.14. So the stated motive pointed past 3.13 rather than to it. At a 3.14 floor SKILL.md:31 becomes false -- `from __future__ import annotations` is described there as mandatory because it makes types-last legal, and at 3.14 the language does that.
